blocks.text: The sum of the terms of a sequence is called the series of the corresponding sequence. For example, \(1 + 2 + 3 + \cdots + n\) is a finite series of the first \(n\) natural numbers.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
A sequence is a list; a series is a sum.
The sequence \(1, 2, 3, \ldots, n\) writes the numbers one after another, separated by commas.
The series \(1 + 2 + 3 + \cdots + n\) adds the same numbers, joined by plus signs.
In this section we learn to find the sum of an arithmetic series quickly, without adding the terms one by one.

The sum of the first \(n\) terms of a series is denoted by \(S_n\). We write
\[S_n = a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_n\]
Here,
\[S_1 = a_1\]
\[S_2 = a_1 + a_2\]
\[S_3 = a_1 + a_2 + a_3\]
\[S_n = a_1 + a_2 + a_3 + \cdots + a_n\]
\(S_n\) is known as the \(n^{\text{th}}\) partial sum.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Partial sums of the A.P. \(3, 7, 11, 15, \ldots\):
\(S_1 = 3\), \(S_2 = 3 + 7 = 10\), \(S_3 = 10 + 11 = 21\), \(S_4 = 21 + 15 = 36\).
Each partial sum is the previous one plus the next term: \(S_n = S_{n-1} + a_n\). So a term can be recovered from two sums:
\[a_n = S_n - S_{n-1},\quad n \ge 2\]
This link between terms and sums is often useful in exercises.
The sum of the terms of an arithmetic sequence is called an arithmetic series.

To develop a formula for the sum of any arithmetic series, consider the sum written forwards (each term is \(d\) more than the one before), where \(a_n = \ell\) is the last term:
\[S_n = a_1 + (a_1 + d) + (a_1 + 2d)\]
\[+ \cdots + (\ell - 2d) + (\ell - d) + \ell\]

Now write the same sum backwards (each term is \(d\) less than the one before):
\[S_n = \ell + (\ell - d) + (\ell + 2d)\]
\[+ \cdots + (a_1 + 2d) + (a_1 + d) + a_1\]

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text:
In the backward sum the book prints the third term as \((\ell + 2d)\). Going backwards every term is \(d\) less than the previous one, so after \(\ell\) and \(\ell - d\) comes \((\ell - 2d)\). The correct line is
\[S_n = \ell + (\ell - d) + (\ell - 2d) + \cdots\]
Only with \(\ell - 2d\) does it pair with \(a_1 + 2d\) to give \(a_1 + \ell\), as the next step needs.

Adding the two lines term by term (first with first, second with second, and so on), every pair gives the same total:
\[2S_n = (a_1 + \ell) + (a_1 + \ell)\]
\[+ \cdots + (a_1 + \ell)\]
\[= n(a_1 + \ell)\]
[We have \(n\) terms of \((a_1 + \ell)\).] Therefore

blocks.text_alt: S n equals n over 2 times, a 1 plus l

blocks.text:
But the last term is the \(n^{\text{th}}\) term, \(\ell = a_1 + (n-1)d\). Substituting \(\ell\) in \(S_n\):
\[S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}[a_1 + a_1 + (n-1)d]\]
Thus,

blocks.text_alt: S n equals n over 2 times, 2 a 1 plus (n minus 1) d

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why does every pair give \(a_1 + \ell\)? Moving one place to the right, the forward term grows by \(d\) and the backward term falls by \(d\); the gain and the loss cancel, so the pair total never changes.
Another way to read \(S_n = \frac{n}{2}(a_1 + \ell)\): \(\frac{a_1 + \ell}{2}\) is the average of the first and last terms, and in an A.P. it is also the average of all the terms. So
sum = (number of terms) \(\times\) (average term).

blocks.title: Key Concept
blocks.text:
The sum \(S_n\) of the first \(n\) terms of an arithmetic series is given by
\[S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}[2a_1 + (n-1)d]\]
or
\[S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}(a_1 + a_n)\]

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text:
Which form to use?
If the last term \(a_n\) is known, use \(S_n = \frac{n}{2}(a_1 + a_n)\).
If the common difference \(d\) is known (and not the last term), use \(S_n = \frac{n}{2}[2a_1 + (n-1)d]\).
Either form gives the same answer, as Example 7 shows. Between them the formulas link five quantities \(a_1, d, n, a_n, S_n\): given any three, the other two can be found.

blocks.title: Example 7
blocks.problem: Find the sum of the first 100 positive integers.
steps:
Given: the series \(1 + 2 + 3 + \cdots + 100\).
To find: \(S_{100}\).
Method: the terms increase by 1 each time, so this is an arithmetic series with \(a_1 = 1\), \(a_n = 100\), \(d = 1\), \(n = 100\). Since both the last term and \(d\) are known, either sum formula works; the book shows both (Method-1 and Method-2).

Method-1: use the first and last terms
\[S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}(a_1 + a_n)\]
\[S_{100} = \dfrac{100}{2}(1 + 100)\]
\[S_{100} = 50(101)\]
\[S_{100} = 5050\]
Why: we know the last term \(a_{100} = 100\), so this form needs no \(d\).

Method-2: use \(a_1\) and \(d\)
\[S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}[2a_1 + (n-1)d]\]
\[S_{100} = \dfrac{100}{2}[2(1) + (100-1)1]\]
\[S_{100} = 50(101)\]
\[S_{100} = 5050\]
Why: \(2(1) + 99(1) = 101\), the same bracket as in Method-1; this form is the one to use when the last term is not given.

Check:
Pair the first and last, second and second last, and so on: \(1 + 100 = 101\), \(2 + 99 = 101\), ..., \(50 + 51 = 101\). There are 50 such pairs, so the sum is \(50 \times 101 = 5050\).

blocks.title: Example 8
blocks.problem:
Find the \(19^{\text{th}}\) term and the partial sum of 19 terms of the arithmetic series:
\[2 + \dfrac{7}{2} + 5 + \dfrac{13}{2} + \cdots\]
steps:
Given: the arithmetic series \(2 + \frac{7}{2} + 5 + \frac{13}{2} + \cdots\)
To find: \(a_{19}\) and \(S_{19}\).
Method: find \(a_1\) and \(d\); use \(a_n = a_1 + (n-1)d\) for the term; then, since the last term \(a_{19}\) is known, use \(S_n = \frac{n}{2}(a_1 + a_n)\).

Step 1: Read \(a_1\) and \(d\)
\[a_1 = 2\]
\[d = a_2 - a_1 = \dfrac{7}{2} - 2 = \dfrac{3}{2}\]
Why: in an A.P. the difference of any two consecutive terms is \(d\). (Check with the next pair: \(5 - \frac{7}{2} = \frac{3}{2}\).)

Step 2: The 19th term
\[a_n = a_1 + (n-1)d\]
\[a_{19} = 2 + (19-1)\dfrac{3}{2}\]
\[= 2 + 18\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)\]
\[= 2 + 27 = 29\]
Why: to reach the 19th term we add \(d\) eighteen times to the first term.

Step 3: The partial sum of 19 terms
\[S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}(a_1 + a_n)\]
\[S_{19} = \dfrac{19}{2}(2 + 29)\]
\[= \dfrac{19}{2}(31) = \dfrac{589}{2}\]
Why: now that \(a_{19}\) is known, the first-and-last form is the shortest.

Check:
With the other form: \(S_{19} = \frac{19}{2}\left[2(2) + 18\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)\right] = \frac{19}{2}(4 + 27) = \frac{19}{2}(31) = \frac{589}{2}\). Same answer.

blocks.title: Example 9
blocks.problem: Find the arithmetic series if its fifth term is 19 and \(S_4 = a_9 + 1\).
steps:
Given: \(a_5 = 19\) and \(S_4 = a_9 + 1\).
To find: the series, that is \(a_1\) and \(d\).
Method: write each condition in terms of \(a_1\) and \(d\) (using \(a_n = a_1 + (n-1)d\) and \(S_n = \frac{n}{2}[2a_1 + (n-1)d]\)), then solve the two equations simultaneously.

Step 1: First condition
\[a_5 = 19\]
\[a_1 + 4d = 19 \quad \text{(i)}\]
Why: \(a_5 = a_1 + (5-1)d\).

Step 2: Second condition
\[S_4 = \dfrac{4}{2}[2a_1 + (4-1)d] = a_9 + 1\]
\[4a_1 + 6d = a_1 + 8d + 1\]
\[3a_1 - 1 = 2d\]
Why: \(S_4 = 2(2a_1 + 3d) = 4a_1 + 6d\) and \(a_9 = a_1 + 8d\). Moving the \(a_1\) terms to the left and the \(d\) terms to the right gives \(3a_1 - 1 = 2d\).

Step 3: Substitute in (i)
\(a_1 + 4d\) is \(a_1 + 2(2d)\), so substituting \(2d = 3a_1 - 1\) in (i):
\[a_1 + 2(3a_1 - 1) = 19\]
\[7a_1 - 2 = 19\]
\[7a_1 = 21 \Rightarrow a_1 = 3\]
Why: replacing \(2d\) leaves one equation in \(a_1\) only.

Step 4: Find \(d\)
From (i):
\[4d = 19 - a_1 = 19 - 3 = 16\]
\[d = 4\]
Why: any one of the equations gives \(d\) once \(a_1\) is known.

Step 5: Write the series
Start at 3 and keep adding 4:
\[3 + 7 + 11 + 15 + 19 + \cdots\]
Why: an arithmetic series is fixed completely by \(a_1\) and \(d\).

blocks.title: Example 10
blocks.problem: How many terms of the series \(-9 - 6 - 3 + 0 + \cdots\) amounts to 66?
steps:
Given: the series \(-9 - 6 - 3 + 0 + \cdots\), i.e. the terms \(-9, -6, -3, 0, \ldots\), and \(S_n = 66\).
To find: \(n\), the number of terms.
Method: \(n\) is the unknown, so put the known \(a_1\), \(d\) and \(S_n\) into \(S_n = \frac{n}{2}[2a_1 + (n-1)d]\); this gives a quadratic equation in \(n\).

Step 1: Read \(a_1\) and \(d\)
\[a_1 = -9\]
\[d = -6 - (-9) = 3\]
Why: \(d\) is any term minus the term before it.

Step 2: Use the sum formula
Let \(S_n = 66\):
\[66 = \dfrac{n}{2}[2(-9) + (n-1)3]\]
\[132 = n[3n - 21]\]
\[44 = n(n - 7)\]
Why: multiply both sides by 2; inside the bracket \(-18 + 3n - 3 = 3n - 21 = 3(n - 7)\), and dividing both sides by 3 gives \(44 = n(n-7)\).

Step 3: Solve the quadratic
\[n^{2} - 7n - 44 = 0\]
\[n = \dfrac{7 \pm \sqrt{49 + 176}}{2}\]
\[= \dfrac{7 \pm \sqrt{225}}{2} = \dfrac{7 \pm 15}{2}\]
\[n = 11,\ -4\]
Why: quadratic formula with \(a = 1\), \(b = -7\), \(c = -44\): \(b^{2} - 4ac = 49 + 176 = 225\). (It also factorizes: \((n - 11)(n + 4) = 0\).)

Step 4: Choose the meaningful root
\(n\) counts terms, so it must be a positive integer. \(n = -4\) is rejected; \(n = 11\).
Why: an algebraic root is not automatically a sensible answer; always test it against the meaning of the unknown.
blocks.answer: \(n = 11\): the sum of eleven terms amounts to 66.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Why can a series that starts with negative terms add up to 66? The terms \(-9, -6, -3\) pull the total down, 0 adds nothing, and the terms \(3, 6, 9\) cancel the negative ones exactly, so \(S_7 = 0\). After that every new term is positive: \(12 + 15 + 18 + 21 = 66\). So \(S_{11} = 66\), exactly what the formula gave.

blocks.title: Example 11
blocks.problem: Find the first three terms of an arithmetic series in which \(a_1 = 9\), \(a_n = 105\) and \(S_n = 741\).
steps:
Given: \(a_1 = 9\), \(a_n = 105\), \(S_n = 741\).
To find: \(a_1, a_2, a_3\).
Method: (Step-I) the form \(S_n = \frac{n}{2}(a_1 + a_n)\) contains only one unknown, \(n\), so it gives \(n\); (Step-II) then \(a_n = a_1 + (n-1)d\) gives \(d\); (Step-III) add \(d\) to get the next terms.

Step-II: Find \(d\)
\[a_n = a_1 + (n-1)d\]
\[105 = 9 + (13-1)d\]
\[96 = 12d\]
\[8 = d\]
Why: now \(n\) is known, so the \(n^{\text{th}}\) term formula has only \(d\) unknown.

Step-III: Use \(d\) to determine \(a_2\) and \(a_3\)
\[a_2 = 9 + 8 = 17\]
\[a_3 = 17 + 8 = 25\]
Why: each term of an A.P. is the previous term plus \(d\).
blocks.answer: The first three terms are 9, 17 and 25.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. A series is the sum of the terms of a sequence; \(S_n\) is the sum of the first \(n\) terms (the \(n^{\text{th}}\) partial sum).
2. Arithmetic series: \(S_n = \frac{n}{2}(a_1 + a_n)\) or \(S_n = \frac{n}{2}[2a_1 + (n-1)d]\).
3. The formula comes from writing the sum forwards and backwards and adding: every pair gives \(a_1 + a_n\).
4. Use the first form when the last term is known, the second when \(d\) is known.
5. If \(n\) is the unknown, the second form gives a quadratic; keep only a positive whole-number root.
6. \(a_n = S_n - S_{n-1}\) for \(n \ge 2\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Writing \(S_n = n[2a_1 + (n-1)d]\): the factor is \(\frac{n}{2}\), not \(n\).
2. Using \(n\) instead of \(n - 1\) inside the bracket: it is \((n-1)d\).
3. Finding \(d\) the wrong way round: \(d = a_2 - a_1\), not \(a_1 - a_2\). In Example 10, \(d = -6 - (-9) = +3\).
4. Keeping a negative or fractional value of \(n\): the number of terms is always a positive integer.
5. Mixing up \(a_n\) (one term) with \(S_n\) (the sum of \(n\) terms).
